demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Rajan arrives for his sessions precisely on time, always in a pressed linen shirt, his hair combed back neatly. He is an interior designer, and he speaks about his clients’ homes with the precision of someone who understands light and space. But his hands shake when he reaches for the water glass on the table. He has been married for twelve years, and his wife, Priya, has noticed the shaking, too. She has also noticed that he no longer sketches in the evenings.

The trauma happened eighteen months ago. Rajan’s younger brother, Arun, died in a scooter accident on a road they had both driven a thousand times. Arun was twenty-seven, a furniture maker, and he was on his way to deliver a walnut dining table he had built for one of Rajan’s clients. They had spoken on the phone forty minutes before the accident. Arun was laughing about a loose drawer. Rajan told him to fix it before delivery. Those were the last words they exchanged. Rajan remembers the call from the hospital as a physical sensation: a cold rush through his arms, the phone slipping, his voice sounding far away.

In the weeks after the funeral, Rajan tried to return to work. He measured a living room for a couple in a new condominium. When he looked through the camera of his tablet to capture the window light, he saw Arun’s face in the reflection of the glass—briefly, but enough to drop the tablet. He began to avoid certain tools: a tape measure, a carpenter’s square. He stopped visiting the hardware store where he and Arun used to buy wood together. He told Priya he was just busy.

At night, Rajan lies awake. Sounds that never bothered him before—the creak of a floorboard, the hum of the refrigerator—now trigger a jolt of alertness. He has started keeping a hammer under the bed. He knows it is irrational, but the feeling of vigilance does not subside. In his dreams, he is on the phone with Arun, and the call keeps dropping, and no matter how many times redials, Arun never picks up. He wakes with his heart pounding and the sense that something terrible is still happening.

His work has become a battlefield of reminders. A client requested a “warm, earthy palette” for a nursery. Rajan immediately thought of the walnut table Arun was delivering. He suggested beige on beige, then excused himself to the bathroom to press his palms against the wall until the dizziness passed. He now volunteers for commercial projects—offices, lobbies—where there are no children’s rooms, no family photos. He tells himself it is a professional preference. He knows it is an avoidance.

At home, Priya tries to reach him. She sits beside him on the sofa and asks about his day. Rajan feels a wall of glass between them. He can see her concern, but he cannot feel it. He responds in short sentences. He has stopped laughing at her jokes. He has stopped going to her family’s gatherings because the noise feels like an attack. He has told her he is tired. That is true, but it is not the whole truth. The truth is that he feels hollowed out, as if the part of him that could connect has been removed.

Yesterday, while measuring a kitchen, Rajan found himself staring at a loose drawer. He stood still for a long time. The client asked if he was okay. He said he had a headache. He came to session today with the same headache. He tells me that he feels like he is living in a house that no longer fits him—every corner reminds him of something missing. He does not talk about forgiveness or healing. He talks about the color of the wallpaper in his childhood bedroom, and how Arun used to draw on the walls with crayon. He says he wishes he could paint over it, but he cannot find the right shade.
